source:
Backyard Monsters is one of the most underappreciated strategy games ever made. It combined Clash of Clans, Factorio, tower defense, RTS, and idle progression years before most mobile games. The core loop was: build a monster base, gather resources, research new monsters, attack other players, and defend your own base while upgrades continued in real time.
I actually think a Roblox spiritual successor could be bigger than the original, because Roblox solves many of the social and multiplayer limitations that Facebook games had.

The Fantasy
You're not building a town.
You're growing a monster civilization hidden inside a suburban backyard.
Imagine:
 • gigantic mushrooms
 • monster nests
 • slime rivers
 • tree forts
 • toy blocks
 • abandoned bicycles
 • sprinklers become rivers
 • garden hoses become bridges
 • sandbox becomes a desert biome
The world feels gigantic because you're tiny.

Enough idle to respect players' time, but not so much that active play feels unnecessary.

Roblox-Specific Improvements
This is where a clone can become something much larger.
Instead of every player living in an isolated instance, imagine an entire persistent neighborhood server with 20-40 players.
Each player owns one backyard, but everyone can:
 • Walk to neighboring yards.
 • Watch live attacks.
 • Trade monster DNA.
 • Visit alliance fortresses.
 • Participate in neighborhood events (like defending against a giant cat invading multiple bases).
This makes the world feel alive in a way the original never could.

Technical Architecture

Server
├── Persistent World
├── Base Simulation
├── Resource Production
├── Combat Engine
├── Pathfinding
├── AI Behavior Trees
├── Research System
├── Alliance System
├── Matchmaking
├── Economy
└── Live Events

Client
├── Building Mode
├── RTS Controls
├── Combat VFX
├── Monster Animation
├── UI
├── Camera
└── Audio

Each player's base is an independently simulated "island" within the larger neighborhood, allowing efficient server performance while still supporting social interactions and live events.

Long-Term Retention
The best strategy games always have goals on multiple timescales:
 • 5-minute session: Collect resources, queue upgrades, check breeding results, attack one nearby base.
 • 30-minute session: Explore a new biome, defeat a boss, redesign your defenses, experiment with a new army composition.
 • Weekly goal: Complete alliance events, unlock a new monster family, climb ranked PvP, finish research branches.
 • Monthly goal: Earn limited seasonal monsters, evolve Ancient monsters, upgrade your fortress, and compete for neighborhood dominance.
The original Backyard Monsters proved that combining base building, asynchronous PvP, and long-term progression was compelling. A modern Roblox version could push that much further by emphasizing collectible monsters with unique AI, exploration beyond the home base, cooperative neighborhood gameplay, and a living world that changes through seasonal events rather than simply recreating the original formula.

answers.ask: Should we build one backyard base first, or the whole neighbourhood world map? Eight expanding world tiers will not fit in a single top-down image, so they would be separate maps.
answers.answer: Build one backyard base first as the playable vertical slice. The wider world map and its expanding tiers can come later as separate maps.

answers.ask: Are the neighbouring players' yards inside the same map as yours, or separate instances you travel to?
answers.answer: Neighbouring players' yards should be separate instances you travel to for scouting and raids, keeping each base focused and readable.

scene_prompt: Create a 3D top-down strategy map for one playable monster civilization base hidden in a suburban backyard, viewed at tiny-creature scale. Center the layout on a Monster Heart, with clear buildable territory branching outward for monster nests and housing, resource extractors and storages, laboratories, breeding caves, spell towers, defensive walls, turrets, traps, acid pools, slime launchers, poison flowers, Venus flytraps, and a future fortress footprint. Surround the base with oversized backyard terrain and landmarks: gigantic mushrooms, tall grass, trees and tree forts, slime rivers, a sprinkler-fed water channel, garden-hose bridges, toy blocks, abandoned bicycles, broken toys, soda cans, old tools, and a sandbox forming a small desert biome. Use height changes, mud, water, cover-providing trees and grass, and open approach routes to shape the terrain. Keep this yard as a focused standalone base map; neighboring player yards are separate destinations rather than visible plots in the same scene.
